name: AI Agent Tool Use and Automation

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Giving an agent real tools

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Describing a tool with a schema
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a tool description with a name, purpose and typed inputs.
This lesson builds toward: For each tool your agent uses, you will write a tool schema with a clear name, purpose and typed inputs, so a model can choose the right tool and arguments.
A model chooses tools from their descriptions. A tool schema is a precise description: a name, one or two sentences on what it does and when to use it, and each input with its type and meaning. Most providers write the inputs in JSON Schema, a standard way to describe data.
Example: name read_csv; description "Read a CSV file from the data folder and return its first 50 rows as text. Use when you need the numbers in a file."; inputs: filename (string, required, a file name in the data folder such as sales-week-42.csv).
Good schemas are small and specific. One tool, one job. Say what the tool returns and when not to use it. Use names that read like actions: read_csv, save_report, not tool1.
Step by step:
- Name the tool with an action word.
- Describe what it does, when to use it and what it returns.
- List each input with its type and whether it is required.
- Keep it to one job.
- Test: give the model a goal and see if it picks the tool correctly.
Words to know:
- Tool schema: a precise description of a tool: its name, purpose and inputs.
- JSON Schema: a standard way to describe the shape of data, such as which fields are text or numbers.
- Argument: a value passed into a tool or function.
Try it now: Write schemas for three tools: read_csv, calculator and save_report. Give a free chatbot the three schemas and the goal "Total last week's sales and save a report", and ask which tool it would call first and with what arguments.
You can now describe a tool so a model can choose it and fill in its inputs correctly.

check.q: What do typed inputs in a tool schema tell the model?
options: How fast the tool runs
Who wrote the tool
What kind of value each input must be, such as text or a number
Which model to use
check.why: Types describe the shape of each input so the model can send the right arguments.

check.q: You want one tool that reads files, sends emails and deletes old reports. What would you do instead?
options: Split it into separate tools that each do one clear job
Keep it, since one tool is simpler
Give it a longer description
Hide the delete part from the schema
check.why: A good tool does one clear job, which makes it easier to describe, check and approve.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Never trust the arguments: validating tool input
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check every argument the model sends before a tool uses it.
This lesson builds toward: Given arguments sent by the model, you will check every argument against an allow list before the tool uses it, refusing bad file types, path tricks and wrong types with a clear error.
The model writes your tool's arguments, and the model can be wrong or be tricked by prompt injection. So the tool, not the model, must enforce the rules. Treat arguments like input from a stranger on the internet.
Check type and shape: is filename a string? Check allowed values: only names ending in .csv, only inside the data folder. Block path tricks: a name like ../../secrets.txt tries to climb out of the folder. In Python: from pathlib import Path, then p = (DATA_DIR / filename).resolve() and refuse if DATA_DIR.resolve() is not in p.parents.
When a check fails, return a clear message, not a crash: "read_csv error: only .csv files in the data folder are allowed". Never run model-written text as code or as a shell command; that is how a small mistake becomes a big one.
Step by step:
- Check the type of each argument.
- Check allowed values: file types, folders, number ranges.
- Resolve file paths and refuse anything outside the allowed folder.
- Return a clear error message on failure.
- Never run model-written text as code or a shell command.
Words to know:
- Validation: checking that input is the right type and within allowed values before using it.
- Path traversal: a trick using ../ in a file name to reach files outside the allowed folder.
- Allow list: a list of the only values that are permitted.
Try it now: Write read_csv with validation. Test it yourself with: 'sales.csv', 'notes.exe', '../secret.txt' and 42. Only the first should read a file; the others should return clear errors.
You can now write tools that check every argument before acting.

check.q: Why must the tool's own code check its arguments?
options: The schema already blocks every bad value
The model may send something unsafe or wrong
It makes the model smarter
It is only needed for write tools
check.why: Only the tool's code can enforce its rules; the model can make mistakes or be tricked.

check.q: read_csv receives the number 42 as a file name. What should happen?
options: Read a file named 42.csv
Turn it into text and keep going
Ask the model to guess the right file
Return a clear error that the file name must be text ending in .csv
check.why: A wrong type is refused with a clear error the model can act on.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Write tools: dry runs and human approval
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Put a write action behind a dry run and a yes/no approval.
This lesson builds toward: For any tool that changes something, you will put the action behind a dry run and a yes/no approval that shows the exact details, so nothing is written until a person says yes.
A write tool changes something: saves a file, sends a message, updates a sheet, spends money. Give write tools two locks. First, a dry run: the tool says exactly what it would do, but does not do it. Make dry run the default, with DRY_RUN = True at the top of your code.
Second, human approval: before the real write, show the person what will happen and ask. In a notebook, answer = input('Save report to reports/week-42.md? yes/no ') and only continue if answer == 'yes'. In a real app, this is an Approve button.
Show the real details in the approval, not a summary the model wrote: the file name, the recipient, the amount. Log every approval and every refusal. If the model asks for the same write again after a no, that is a sign to stop the run.
Step by step:
- Mark each tool READ or WRITE.
- Give every write tool a dry-run mode, on by default.
- Before a real write, show the exact details and ask yes or no.
- Write only on yes, and log the answer.
- Stop the run if the model retries a refused write.
Words to know:
- Dry run: a practice run that shows what would happen without doing it.
- Approval gate: a point where a person must say yes before an action happens.
Try it now: Write save_report(filename, text) with validation (only .md or .txt, only in a reports folder), a dry-run default and a yes/no approval. Try it with DRY_RUN on, then off, answering no once and yes once.
You can now add write tools that only act after a dry run and a human yes.

check.q: What does a dry run do?
options: Shows what would happen without doing it
Runs the action twice to be sure
Deletes the old file first
Saves a backup copy of the model
check.why: A dry run lets a person see the result before anything changes.

check.q: The approval prompt only says "Proceed? yes/no". What would you change?
options: Nothing, it is short and clear
Make the agent answer yes itself
Show the exact file name and text that will be saved
Remove the approval to save time
check.why: A person can only approve well when they see the exact details.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Triggers, schedules and safe re-runs
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a trigger for an agent and make re-runs safe.
This lesson builds toward: Given a task that runs regularly, you will choose a trigger and make the automation safe to re-run, so a second run for the same period creates no duplicate.
An automation is an agent that starts on its own. A trigger starts it: a schedule (every Monday at 8 am), an event (a new file in a folder, a new form response) or a button someone presses.
Automations get re-run: a schedule fires twice, a run fails halfway and you start it again. Design for it. Idempotent means running it twice gives the same result as once. Name outputs by their period (reports/week-42.md) and check before writing: if the report exists, stop or ask, instead of making a copy.
Ways to schedule: on your own computer, Windows Task Scheduler or cron on Mac and Linux can run a Python script; no-code tools like Zapier, Make and n8n run workflows on triggers; cloud services have schedulers too. Colab is for building and testing, not for running on a schedule. Check each tool's current free limits on its own site.
Step by step:
- Pick the trigger: schedule, event or button.
- Name each output by its period, like week-42.
- Before writing, check whether the output already exists.
- If it does, stop or ask; never duplicate.
- Choose where it will run, and check that tool's limits.
Words to know:
- Trigger: the event that starts an automation.
- Idempotent: safe to run more than once: the second run changes nothing extra.
- Cron: a scheduler on Mac and Linux that runs commands at set times.
Try it now: Change save_report so the file name includes the week number, and so a second run for the same week stops with "Report for week 42 already exists". Run it twice to prove it.
You can now choose a trigger and make an automation safe to run more than once.

check.q: What does it mean that an automation is idempotent?
options: It runs only once a year
Running it twice gives the same result as running it once
It never needs a trigger
It always asks for approval
check.why: Idempotent jobs can be re-run safely without making duplicates.

check.q: Your weekly job ran twice by mistake and made two reports. What would you change?
options: Run it less often
Delete reports by hand each week
Turn off the log
Name the report by week and stop if that week's report already exists
check.why: A week-based name plus an exists check makes re-runs safe.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Connecting tools with MCP
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain what MCP is and decide when to use an MCP server.
This lesson builds toward: Given a tool you want to share with AI apps, you will explain what an MCP server does and decide when to use one, naming the approval and checking rules you would keep.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to outside systems: files, databases, calendars, search tools. Its own site compares it to a USB-C port for AI: build a connection once and many AI apps can use it.
In MCP, a server offers tools and data; a client (inside an AI app such as Claude, ChatGPT or a code editor like VS Code) connects to it and lets the model use them. You can use ready-made servers or write your own small server in Python that wraps tools like your read_csv.
MCP does not make a tool safe by itself. Every rule from Chapter 1 still applies: check arguments, least privilege, approval for writes. Install servers only from sources you trust, because a server runs with whatever access you give it. Read the MCP security best-practices page before connecting anything private.
Words to know:
- MCP: Model Context Protocol: an open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data.
- MCP server: a program that offers tools or data to AI apps through MCP.
- MCP client: the part of an AI app that connects to MCP servers.
Official sources:
- Model Context Protocol: What is MCP?
Try it now: Read the MCP introduction page. Then write three sentences: which of your tools you would offer through an MCP server, which AI app would use it, and which approval rule you would keep.
You can now explain MCP servers and clients and decide when connecting a tool through MCP makes sense.

options: A program that offers tools and data to AI apps in a standard way
A model that writes code
A cloud folder for reports
A kind of API key
check.why: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way to connect tools and data to AI apps.

check.q: You offer save_report through an MCP server. What happens to its argument checks and approval?
options: They can be removed, since MCP handles safety
They move to the AI app
You keep them in the tool
Only the approval stays
check.why: MCP connects tools; it does not replace the checks and approvals in your own code.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Building the weekly report automation
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Put the tools, the loop and the safety rules together into one automation.
This lesson builds toward: Given read, calculator and save tools, you will build and test the weekly report automation end to end, with a full run log and bad data reported, not ignored.
Now assemble everything. Tools: read_csv (read, validated), calculator (read, validated), save_report (write: validated, dry run, approval, no duplicates). The loop from course 3 with a step limit and a log. A system prompt from course 2 with the goal: summarize the week and save a report.
Make a small made-up file to test with, such as data/sales-week-42.csv with columns day, item, amount. Never test with real customer or personal data.
Run it start to finish. Read the log: did it read before it calculated? Did it ask before saving? Run it a second time for the same week: it must not make a duplicate. Then try a file with a bad row (a word where a number should be) and check it reports the problem instead of guessing.
Step by step:
- Create a made-up CSV in a data folder.
- Register the three tools with their schemas.
- Run the loop with a step limit and a log.
- Approve the save once; run again to test no duplicates.
- Test a file with a bad row.
Words to know:
- Test data: made-up data used to check a program without risking real information.
- End-to-end test: running the whole automation from start to finish.
Try it now: Final task: build the weekly report agent with read_csv, calculator and save_report (validated, dry run by default, yes/no approval, no duplicates). Run it on a made-up CSV, run it again for the same week, and save the log of the full run.
You can now turn an agent into a safe, repeatable automation with real tools.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Tools described A tool has no schema or a vague name or purpose. read_csv, calculator and save_report each have a name, purpose and typed inputs. Descriptions are clear enough that the model picks the right tool first time. Arguments checked save_report accepts any file name or folder. Only .txt or .md files, only in the reports folder; bad input gets a clear error. read_csv is checked the same way and the errors are tested. Dry run and approval The report is written without a dry run or a yes. Dry run is on by default and "Save report? yes/no" is asked before writing. The approval shows the exact file name and a preview of the text. Safe re-run A second run for the same week makes a duplicate report. A second run for the same week stops without a duplicate. It says clearly which week's report already exists. Full run logged No log, or the run did not finish. The log shows one full run from reading the CSV to the approval. The summary reports any bad rows in the data. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is an end-to-end test of your automation?
options: Testing only the calculator
Running the whole automation from start to finish
Reading the code out loud
Testing the model in a chatbot
check.why: End to end means every part runs together, the way it will for real.

check.q: Your CSV has the word "none" where a sales number should be. What should the agent do?
options: Report the problem in its summary
Count it as zero without saying so
Skip the whole file
Guess a number
check.why: A good agent reports bad data instead of hiding it.
